content: Transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTNB), also referred to as transitory tachypnea of the newborn, is a respiratory condition that occurs in neonates shortly after birth. It is characterized by a period of abnormally rapid breathing, defined as a respiratory rate exceeding the normal range of 40 to 60 breaths per minute for newborns. This condition is thought to result from retained fetal lung fluid and is more commonly observed in infants born at or beyond 35 weeks of gestation, particularly those delivered via cesarean section without preceding labor. Typically, TTNB resolves spontaneously within 24 to 48 hours. Management is supportive and may involve the administration of supplemental oxygen and antibiotics. On chest X-ray, findings indicative of TTNB include hyperinflation of the lungs, prominent pulmonary vascular markings, flattening of the diaphragm, and the presence of fluid in the horizontal fissure. Pathophysiology 1. The higher incidence of TTNB in neonates delivered by cesarean section has led to the hypothesis that the condition arises from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid via the pulmonary lymphatic system. This retained fluid increases airway resistance and decreases lung compliance, contributing to the respiratory symptoms. 2. Pulmonary immaturity has also been proposed as a contributing factor. In some affected neonates, levels of phosphatidylglycerol, a marker of lung maturity, have been found to be absent or insufficient. 3. Mild surfactant deficiency has been suggested as another potential causative factor in the development of TTNB. Diagnosis Chest X-ray Radiographic findings consistent with pulmonary edema in TTNB include airspace opacities, prominent interstitial markings, indistinct and prominent pulmonary vasculature, pleural effusions, and cardiomegaly. The lung volumes may appear normal or increased.
